interactions.summary: Students test possible explanations for Virgil's knowledge, and Jiang gravitates toward a poetology answer: poets channel divine fire and can carry truths larger than their own conscious understanding.

claims.claim: Jiang rejects the idea that Dante is simply ventriloquizing Virgil, insisting that Dante the son would not presumptuously teach Virgil truths he has not yet learned.
A student suggests Lucifer may know the truth well enough to distort it, which Jiang accepts as a promising line for explaining Virgil's contact with truth.
Jiang ultimately reframes the question through poetry: a poet is a vessel for divine fire and can channel truths beyond full conscious comprehension.
Under this model, Virgil's possession of truth would imply that the Aeneid itself contains divine material even if Virgil deployed it wrongly.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang defines the poet as a vessel of divine fire who may speak more truth than he can consciously explain.
signature_moments.source_phrase: a poet is a vessel for the divine fire
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It becomes the central engine for explaining both Virgil's dangerous power and Dante's later authority.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Jiang's term for the sacred imaginative power poets channel from beyond themselves.

chronology_notes.note: The class moves from theology and Lucifer speculation into a poetics of divine channeling that will ground the later charge against Virgil.
